newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zapatista leader seeks "definitive peace" in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Zapatista leader seeks "definitive peace" in Mexico.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-10-16

text.p: Zapatista rebel leader Subcommander Marcos on Wednesday called on the Mexican government to help restart stalled peace talks and reach a "definitive peace" in the southern state of Chiapas.

Marcos, the enigmatic, pipe-smoking leader who always wears a ski mask in public to hide his identity, made his comments in a meeting with peace mediators in an effort to get derailed peace talks back on track.

"We want to find a formula that will push the dialogue forward rapidly in a more serious way and in the short term produce better results and a definitive peace," Marcos told the mediators. Both sides are scheduled to meet through Thursday.

The Zapatista National Liberation Army broke off negotiations with the government on Sept. 2, charging that government negotiators were dragging their feet and that some held racist attitudes against the mostly Mayan Indian rebels, who launched their uprising on New Year's Day 1994.
Marcos and 16 rebel commanders arrived in this colonial city late on Tuesday after leaving their weapons behind in their remote Lacandona jungle bases. They were escorted by the Mexican Red Cross.
"We are here to undertake a new effort, a new road, to have the certainty of once again having a diologue," said Jose Narro, president of the government peace delegation.
Fighting between Zapatistas and government troops was halted after a few days in 1994, but at least 150 people were killed. A ceasefire has held throughout the 18-month-long peace process.
